t: Find the Maximum Number of Marked Indices — Sorted Two Pointers
o: Repeatedly pair two unmarked indices with 2·nums[i] ≤ nums[j] and mark both; maximize the number of marked indices (always even). In [9,2,5,4] all four can be paired; in [3,5,2,4] only one pair (2,4) exists; in [7,6,8] none. Since marking happens in pairs, the answer is even, and pairing is easiest after sorting: small values should pair with large values.
k: Sort and greedily match the smallest unmarked values against the largest; if a match fails, the large value is useless for anyone smaller.

a.n: Approach 1: Sort + two pointers over halves
a.i: Sort nums. Use pointer i over the lower half and j over the upper half (starting near the middle). Whenever 2·nums[i] ≤ nums[j], mark both and advance both; otherwise only advance j, because nums[j] cannot pair with any remaining (even larger) i-value. Each successful match contributes 2 to the answer. This greedy is optimal: exchanging partners never enables more pairs.
s: Set i = 0, j = ⌈n/2⌉ (start of upper region).
While j < n: if 2·nums[i] ≤ nums[j], i++; j++. Otherwise j++.
a.t: O(n log n) — sorting dominates; the two-pointer sweep is linear.

a.n: Approach 2: Binary search on the answer
a.i: Feasibility of marking 2k indices is monotone: if 2k indices can be marked, so can 2(k−1). To check k pairs, sort and test whether the k smallest values can each be doubled into one of the k largest values (greedy matching). Binary search k over [0, ⌊n/2⌋].
s: Binary search on p = number of pairs.
check(p): for t in 0..p−1 require 2·nums[t] ≤ nums[n−p+t] (after sorting).
a.t: O(n log² n) — O(log n) binary-search steps, each an O(n) feasibility check (plus the initial sort).

w: Use Approach 1 — it's shorter and faster. Why start j at the middle: pairing within the same half can never beat cross-half pairing, since the t-th smallest viable partner must exceed the t-th smallest value. Watch overflow with 2·nums[i] in C++/Java (use long). Edge cases: n = 1 (answer 0), all-equal arrays (only 0 pairs since 2x ≤ x fails for x ≥ 1). Follow-up: output the actual pairs.
